editorial_reason: Read Stacks 10.167, a short section proving that Cohen–Macaulayness of Noetherian algebras is preserved under finitely generated field extensions. The introductory sentence expressly notes that the title 'geometrically Cohen–Macaulay' is a misnomer here, and no distinct geometric Cohen–Macaulay definition is introduced.

Read Stacks 10.102 including Definition 10.102.5 and its surrounding reduction of finite free complexes, which explicitly introduces a rank via exterior powers and the ideal of maximal minors. The remaining material proves an exactness criterion, not a new meaning of exactness.

definitions.text: For a homomorphism φ:R^m→R^n of finite free modules, its rank is the largest integer r for which the induced exterior-power map ∧^rφ is nonzero (and is zero when φ itself is zero).
definitions.context_hint: Commutative algebra: rank of a finite-free-module map

definitions.text: For a homomorphism φ:R^m→R^n of rank r, its maximal-rank determinantal ideal I(φ) is the ideal of R generated by all r×r minors of a matrix representing φ; by convention it equals R when r=0.
definitions.context_hint: Commutative algebra: ideal of maximal nonzero-size minors

editorial_reason: Read Stacks 4.31, Definitions 4.31.1 and 4.31.2 together with Example 4.31.3. This section defines a final object in a (2,1)-category and a 2-fibre product relative to invertible 2-morphisms, unlike a strict ordinary pullback.

definitions.text: A final object T of a (2,1)-category C is an object such that, for every Y in C, there is a 1-morphism Y→T and any two such 1-morphisms are connected by exactly one 2-morphism.
definitions.context_hint: Higher category theory: final object of a (2,1)-category

definitions.text: For 1-morphisms X→Z←Y in a (2,1)-category, a 2-fibre product X×_Z Y is a terminal object, in the 2-categorical sense, among objects W equipped with maps W→X and W→Y and an invertible 2-morphism between the two resulting maps W→Z.
definitions.context_hint: Higher category theory: 2-fibre product in a (2,1)-category

definitions.text: For functors F:A→C and G:B→C, their iso-comma category A×_C B has triples (a,b,α:F(a)≅G(b)) as objects and compatible pairs of arrows in A and B as morphisms.
definitions.context_hint: Category theory: iso-comma construction of a 2-fibre product

editorial_reason: Read Stacks Topology 5.25, which explicitly characterizes the Stone–Čech compactification by its universal factorization for maps to Hausdorff quasi-compact spaces; the proof constructs it using products of target compactifications.

definitions.text: A Stone–Čech compactification of a topological space X (in this source's universal-map sense) is a continuous map η:X→βX into a compact Hausdorff space βX such that every continuous f:X→K with K compact Hausdorff factors uniquely through a continuous map βX→K.
definitions.source_section: Section 5.25 introductory universal property and subsequent product construction
definitions.context_hint: Topology: Stone–Čech compactification by universal property

editorial_reason: Read Stacks 10.159 on constructing flat local ring maps with a prescribed residue-field extension. Its main statement, Lemma 10.159.1, is an existence and construction theorem using flat local maps, filtered colimits and Zorn's lemma, without introducing a distinct new defined object for the heading.

Read Stacks 10.30, 'More on images', consisting of technical results on images of finite-type maps of spectra, constructible subsets, and generic finite presentation. The section adds no standalone notion titled 'more on images'; image and constructible subsets were previously defined.

Read Stacks Fields 9.20 Definition 9.20.1 and the associated basis-independent multiplication-operator interpretation; trace and norm are two different field-extension invariants and should be separate meanings.

definitions.text: For a finite extension L/K and α∈L, the field trace Tr_{L/K}(α) is the trace over K of the K-linear endomorphism of L given by multiplication x↦αx.
definitions.context_hint: Field theory: trace of an element in a finite field extension

definitions.text: For a finite extension L/K and α∈L, the field norm N_{L/K}(α) is the determinant over K of the multiplication-by-α endomorphism L→L.
definitions.context_hint: Field theory: norm of an element in a finite field extension

editorial_reason: Read Stacks 10.148 Definition 10.148.1 and Lemma 10.148.3. Formal unramifiedness has a unique-lifting condition for square-zero extensions and an equivalent vanishing condition on Kähler differentials.

definitions.text: A ring homomorphism R→S is formally unramified if, for every R-algebra A and square-zero ideal I⊆A, any R-algebra map S→A/I admits at most one lift to an R-algebra map S→A.
definitions.context_hint: Commutative algebra: formally unramified ring homomorphism

definitions.text: A ring homomorphism R→S is formally unramified exactly when its module of Kähler differentials Ω_{S/R} is zero.
definitions.context_hint: Commutative algebra: differential characterization of formal unramifiedness

editorial_reason: Read Stacks Fields 9.23 on the complex numbers and its argument proving the fundamental theorem of algebra. It proves C is algebraically closed using Galois theory and an odd-degree-polynomial argument, but does not define a new meaning of 'complex numbers' here; that construction must be sourced from an introductory definition elsewhere.

Read Stacks 10.137, Definition 10.137.1 and surrounding results. The Stacks criterion for a smooth ring map combines finite presentation and a naive cotangent complex quasi-isomorphic to a finite projective module in degree zero.

definitions.text: A homomorphism R→S of commutative rings is smooth if S is finitely presented as an R-algebra and the naive cotangent complex NL_{S/R} is quasi-isomorphic to a finite projective S-module in degree zero.

editorial_reason: Read Stacks 10.18, Definition 10.18.1, which gives equivalent characterizations of local rings in terms of unique maximal ideals and nonunits. This permits two logically equivalent formulations rather than two meanings.

definitions.text: A nonzero commutative ring R is local if it possesses exactly one maximal ideal.
Equivalently, a nonzero commutative ring R is local if the set of its nonunits is an ideal; this ideal is necessarily the ring's unique maximal ideal.
definitions.context_hint: Commutative algebra: nonunit characterization of a local ring

editorial_reason: Read Stacks 10.25 on zerodivisors and total rings of fractions. It defines the total quotient ring by inverting all nonzerodivisors and distinguishes the zero-divisor subset from its complement, the multiplicative set of regular elements.

definitions.text: An element r of a commutative ring R is a zerodivisor when some nonzero element s∈R satisfies rs=0; a nonzerodivisor is an element for which multiplication by r on R is injective.
definitions.source_section: Section 10.25 introductory discussion of zero divisors
definitions.context_hint: Commutative algebra: zerodivisor and regular element

definitions.text: The total quotient ring Q(R) of a commutative ring R is the localization S^{-1}R at the multiplicative set S of all nonzerodivisors of R, allowing fractions with any regular denominator.
definitions.source_section: Section 10.25 introductory total ring of fractions construction
